title: News travels fast
topic: News, media and how to spot fake stories

vocab.name: News and media
words: news about something that is happening right now
*Breaking news*: a storm has hit the coast.
a person who saw an event happen
An *eyewitness* filmed the accident on her phone.
the title of a news story
The *headline* said 'Teen saves dog from river'.
a person who writes or reports the news
broadcast at the same time as it happens
They showed the match *live* on TV.
a person who reads the news on TV or radio
The *news presenter* smiled and said good evening.
an account of an event; to tell people about it
She wrote a *report* about the protest.
a journalist who goes to places to collect news
The *reporter* is standing outside the stadium.
a person or document that gives information
Always check the *source* of a story.
We'll give you an *update* in an hour.

vocab.name: Compound nouns: media
words: a famous person who affects what followers buy or think
A *celebrity influencer* posted about the new trainers.
online content designed to make you click
'You won't believe what happened next!' is typical *clickbait*.
a belief that a secret group is behind an event
There's a *conspiracy theory* that the moon landing was fake.
important political and social events happening now
We discuss *current affairs* in class every Monday.
false stories that look like real news
*Fake news* spreads quickly on social media.
a company that publishes news (newspaper, channel, website)
Which *media outlet* published the story first?
a list of updates on a social media app
My *newsfeed* is full of football videos.
a system that makes you pay to read content online
I couldn't read the article because of the *paywall*.
a website or app for sharing content
TikTok is a popular *social media platform*.
a way of communicating with images

slides.sub: News travels fast: what did the eyewitness say?
slides.hook: Think of a piece of breaking news you heard recently. Who said it? Can you report what they said?

p: Direct speech repeats the exact words. Reported speech tells someone what another person said, usually with 'said' or 'told'. Journalists use it all the time!
ex: Direct: 'I **saw** the fire,' the eyewitness said.
Reported: The eyewitness said that she **had seen** the fire.

rows: present simple: 'I work for a big media outlet.'
past simple: He said he worked for a big media outlet.
past continuous: She said she was reporting live.
past perfect: He said he had seen the accident.
past perfect: They said they had published an update.
will: 'The story will be the main headline.'
would: She said the story would be the main headline.
could: He said he could check the source.
the next day / the following day
the day before / the previous day
slides.note: Pronouns change too: 'I'm a journalist,' Ana said → Ana said she was a journalist.

p: say + (that) + clause: He said (that) it was fake news.
tell + person + (that) + clause: He told me (that) it was fake news.
ex: The news presenter **said** the story was clickbait.
The news presenter **told us** the story was clickbait.

slides.title: Fire at the shopping centre
text: An eyewitness **told** our reporter that she **had seen** smoke at about 6 p.m. She **said** that people **were running** out of the building.
A firefighter **said** that nobody **had been** hurt. He **told** journalists that they **would give** an update the next day.
The mayor **said** that the centre **could** open again that week. Some social media posts claimed it was an attack, but that was fake news.

items: The reporter said me that the road was closed.
The reporter told me that the road was closed.
He told that the headline was wrong.
He said that the headline was wrong.
tell needs an object (me / us / them).
They said they will publish the story tomorrow.
They said they would publish the story the next day.
will → would; tomorrow → the next day.

slides.q: 'I am watching the breaking news.' → He said he ___ the breaking news.
'We have published the headline.' → They said they ___ the headline.

p: Tenses move one step back into the past.
'that' is optional after say and tell.

grammar.title: Reported questions, requests and commands
grammar.short: asked if..., told me to..., asked me not to...

slides.hook: If you could interview a famous news presenter or influencer, what would you ask them?

p: Use asked + if / whether + statement word order. No question mark, no do / does / did.
ex: 'Are you a reporter?' → She asked me **if I was** a reporter.
'Did you see the accident?' → The police asked the eyewitness **whether she had seen** the accident.

p: Use asked + question word + statement word order.
ex: 'Where do you get your news?' → He asked me **where I got** my news.
'What happened?' → The journalist asked **what had happened**.
'Why did you share that post?' → My teacher asked **why I had shared** that post.

rows: The teacher asked us to check our sources.
She told us not to share fake news.
'Turn off your newsfeed for an hour.'
He told me to turn off my newsfeed for an hour.

slides.title: We met a news presenter!
text: Last week we interviewed Clara Ruiz, a news presenter on local TV. First, we **asked her how** she **had become** a journalist. She said she had started on the school newspaper!
Then Leo **asked whether** she **was** nervous when she was live on TV. She laughed and said 'Always!'
At the end, she **told us to read** news from different sources and **asked us not to believe** every headline on social media.

items: She asked me where did I get my news.
She asked me where I got my news.
He asked me was the story true.
He asked me if the story was true.
She told me don't click on the clickbait.
She told me not to click on the clickbait.
